To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the language of a graph is prefix-free, (b) a finite language can represent a finite graph, (c) a finite automaton can represent a finite language, and (d) a finite automata can therefore represent a finite graph.

(1) the concatenation of prefix-free languages is a natural way of representing the substitution of graphs, (2) this representation is compact in that it uses the same number of bits to represent the same graph, (3) this representation is also efficient in that it uses only a constant number of extra bits, (4) this representation is natural in that it is based on the well-understood notion of language concatenation.

(1) finite languages are an alternative to adjacency matrices, (2) finite languages are a compact and natural way of specifying finite graphs, (3) finite automata are a compact and efficient way of specifying finite languages, and (4) the fundamental operations of finite automata and finite languages are the operations of graph substitution and graph concatenation, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: what is the most general way to represent finite graphs?
the following question: How can finite languages (sets of strings) be used to compactly specify graphs?
a new way to specify graphs and the relationships between the operations of concatenation and substitution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
languages are to graphs as trees are to trees.
, with the positional method, languages can be viewed and used as graphs, and graphs can be viewed and represented as languages.
, in a certain precise sense, languages are graphs, and graphs are languages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found an elegant, simple and powerful method to represent graphs.
we show how to specify graphs through languages, and how to specify languages through graphs.
we have introduced a new way to represent finite graphs and have shown that it has a number of interesting properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
languages can serve as a unifying representation of graphs and that this representation is well-suited for the specification of large graphs.
languages and graphs can be seen as two sides of the same coin.
languages are a powerful and elegant tool for the specification of graphs.
